title: Performance, Fairness, and Explainability in AI-Based Credit Scoring: A Systematic Literature Review
authors: Bahlool, R.; Hewahi, N.; Elmedany, W.
venue: Journal of Risk and Financial Management
tldr: Systematic review of 43 peer-reviewed studies reveals that performance, fairness, and explainability in AI credit scoring are predominantly addressed in isolation rather than jointly optimized.
problem_and_motivation: Research on AI-based credit scoring remains fragmented, with performance, fairness, and explainability most often addressed in isolation rather than as jointly optimized objectives. No unified framework co-optimizes all three pillars while incorporating regulatory compliance and human-in-the-loop oversight. This gap limits the practical deployment of responsible credit scoring models in regulated, high-stakes lending environments.
approach: Systematic literature review following PRISMA 2020 guidelines with a PICOC-guided search strategy across IEEE Xplore, Scopus, Web of Science, and ScienceDirect databases.
Boolean search string combined credit scoring, machine learning or deep learning, and explainable AI or fairness terms, restricted to peer-reviewed publications from 2020 to 2025.
Inclusion required studies to address credit scoring in consumer or lending contexts and cover at least one of performance, fairness, or explainability.
A customized 3Rs&&Q appraisal framework with eight sub-metrics (0-3 scale, max 24) was used for quality assessment and study inclusion.
436 initial records were screened through title, abstract, and full-text stages, with 58 reports assessed and 15 excluded for low quality scores (≤8).
Data extraction was performed by one reviewer using Zotero for reference management and Excel for coding, with cross-checking against original articles.
Three research questions targeted performance-explainability trade-offs (RQ1), bias mitigation strategies (RQ2), and regulatory and HITL integration (RQ3).
Pairwise intersection analysis was used to quantify co-occurrence of dimensions across the 43 included studies.
findings: Explainability showed the strongest research expansion between 2023 and 2024, becoming the dominant pillar of recent credit scoring research.
Performance gap between interpretable and black-box models is only 0.14–0.21% in annual return on investment, indicating the trade-off is largely assumed rather than empirically measured.
Out of 43 included studies, only 10 explicitly measured effectiveness of fairness mitigation strategies, representing 23.25% of the total reviewed literature.
The BASL rejection inference framework recovered up to 36% of performance loss due to sampling bias while simultaneously improving fairness.
num: 78.9% of included studies were published between 2023 and 2024, confirming a surge in research across all investigated dimensions.
num: 95.4% of included studies were journal articles, with 4.6% conference papers, from 6 distinct publisher families.
Fairness constraints reduce accuracy progressively as they tighten, confirming a proportional relationship between accuracy and fairness violations.
No universally dominant mitigation strategy exists across pre-processing, in-processing, and post-processing stages of the deployment pipeline.
key_figures_tables: Figure 2: Conceptual framework showing intersections among performance, fairness, and explainability in AI credit scoring → Each overlap corresponds to one of three research questions guiding the review.
Figure 3: PRISMA 2020 flow diagram → Documents screening from 436 records to 43 included studies through identification, screening, and eligibility stages.
Figure 4: Topic coverage by year → Shows a clear shift from performance-focused research toward explainability and fairness-aware credit scoring from 2023 onward.
Table 5: Pairwise intersections between dimensions → Fairness and protected attributes co-occur in 21 papers, the largest intersection found.
Table 6: Interpretable vs. black-box model performance comparison → Marginal AUC differences suggest the explainability–performance trade-off is rarely quantified.

definitions.definition: Explainable AI, techniques that clarify the rationale and reasoning behind AI-generated outcomes.
Human-in-the-loop, a governance approach embedding human judgment throughout model development and deployment.
Know Your Customer, a mandatory process for lending institutions to capture personal and repayment records.
Equal Credit Opportunity Act, a US law prohibiting discriminatory lending based on personal characteristics.
General Data Protection Regulation, EU privacy law intersecting with fairness obligations in credit scoring.
Fair Interpolation Method, an algorithm interpolating between incompatible fairness criteria using optimal transport.
Bias-Aware Self-Learning, a semi-supervised framework that iteratively labels unlabeled data to reduce sampling bias.
Relevance, Rigor, Reproducibility, and Quality, a custom appraisal framework for evaluating study inclusion.
Population, Intervention, Comparison, Outcome, and Context, a framework used to formulate research questions.
Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses, a guideline framework for transparent review reporting.
Area Under the ROC Curve, a standard metric for evaluating binary classification model performance.
SHapley Additive exPlanations, a post-hoc method for explaining individual predictions via feature attributions.
Local Interpretable Model-agnostic Explanations, a post-hoc technique for explaining individual predictions.

topic_relevance.contribution_to_field: This systematic literature review synthesizes 43 peer-reviewed studies to map the intersection of performance, fairness, and explainability in AI-based credit scoring. It demonstrates that these three pillars are predominantly addressed in isolation, with limited empirical evidence for the commonly assumed performance-explainability trade-off. The review provides a governance-oriented framework for understanding how regulatory requirements, fairness mitigation strategies, and human-in-the-loop oversight interact across the deployment pipeline. By consolidating empirical and conceptual evidence, the paper identifies the most significant gap as the absence of unified co-optimization frameworks that treat all three pillars as interdependent constraints throughout the model lifecycle.
directly_justifies: The performance gap between interpretable and black-box models is marginal, primarily determined by risk tolerance rather than measurable predictive loss.
Fairness is tunable but no universally dominant mitigation strategy exists across pre-processing, in-processing, and post-processing stages.
Only 23.25% of included studies explicitly measure fairness mitigation effectiveness despite fairness being a long-standing concern.
Explainability became the dominant research pillar from 2023 onward, driven by regulatory frameworks such as the EU AI Act and ECOA.
The trade-off between performance and fairness is consistently confirmed across the literature as a multi-objective optimization problem.
limits: The review was conducted by a single reviewer, potentially limiting inter-rater reliability in study screening and quality assessment.
No public registry of the review protocol was established, reducing pre-registration transparency.
Coverage is concentrated on Western and ASEAN regulatory contexts with limited evidence from other jurisdictional settings.
Individual fairness was mentioned only conceptually without empirical implementation across included studies.
The 3Rs&&Q framework thresholds were determined a priori based on distribution rather than validated domain-specific criteria.
topic_relevance.topic_mapping_rationale: All 14 topic domains were systematically scanned for citeable claims. Domain 4 (Landscape and Gaps in Existing Systems) was flagged as highly relevant because the paper maps the current research landscape and identifies fragmentation across performance, fairness, and explainability. Domain 6 (Predictive Modeling) was assigned high relevance due to extensive analysis of interpretable versus black-box model trade-offs. Domain 8 (Anomaly Detection) received medium relevance because class imbalance and rejection inference are discussed as detection challenges. Domain 10 (Data Privacy and Security) was assigned high relevance given the paper's coverage of GDPR, ECOA, and protected attribute handling. Domain 12 (Evaluation Frameworks) received high relevance for the 3Rs&&Q appraisal framework and comparative model evaluation. Domain 14 (ML Deployment) was assigned medium relevance for discussion of deployment pipeline stages. Domains 1–3 (Filipino demographics, culturally specific practices, expense categorization) were rejected as the paper does not address personal finance behaviors or Filipino-specific contexts. Domain 7 (Budgeting Strategies) was rejected because budgeting optimization is not addressed. Domain 9 (Mobile-First Design) was rejected because the paper is a systematic review with no mobile-specific design discussion. Domain 11 (Engagement and Retention) was rejected because engagement dynamics are not analyzed. Domain 13 (Savings and Debt Management) was rejected because the paper focuses on credit scoring rather than personal savings or debt management. Overall, the paper's topical coverage centers on the algorithmic evaluation landscape, regulatory frameworks, and fairness mitigation in AI-based credit scoring systems.

limitations: Single-reviewer screening and quality assessment may introduce assessor subjectivity despite evidence-driven scoring rules.
The review protocol was not registered in PROSPERO or any other public registry.
Fairness metrics are analyzed at a conceptual level without empirical benchmarking across datasets in the review itself.
Individual fairness is mentioned only conceptually in a few studies without empirical implementation.
The scope excludes corporate lending and SME credit scoring, limiting generalizability to consumer lending contexts.
remember_this: Performance gap between interpretable and black-box models is only 0.14–0.21% in annual return on investment, making the trade-off largely assumed.
Explainability became the dominant research pillar from 2023 onward, surpassing fairness and human intervention in publication volume.
No universally dominant fairness mitigation strategy exists; each exhibits distinct strengths and limitations across pipeline stages.
Only 10 of 43 studies explicitly measure fairness mitigation effectiveness, indicating fairness remains underexplored relative to explainability.
A unified co-optimizing framework treating performance, fairness, and explainability as interdependent constraints is absent from the literature.
